item.title: Misophonia Has It's Own Neural Signature
item.description:
Misophonia

Misophonia Has It's Own Neural Signature

An interview with Dr. Heather Hansen on her misophonia research.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Misophonia's neural signature is different than what we see in anxiety and other disorders.
  • This adds important evidence to the notion that misophonia is a standalone disorder.
  • The anterior insula, part of the salience network, is highly involved in misophonia.
  • In the study, the more connectivity from the anterior insula is associated with more severe misophonia.

I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. Heather Hansen about her latest work, which adds support to the notion that misophonia is a stand-alone disorder. Dr. Hansen runs the Cognition and Auditory Perception of Everyday Sounds (CAPES) Lab in the Department of Psychological Sciences at William & Mary College. For her recent study, Hansen and colleagues analyzed the brain connectivity of 162 adults as a function of misophonia severity. Their findings highlight numerous important issues about misophonia, bringing us further in our understanding of misophonia as a disorder that crosses disciplines but is simultaneously a unique disorder.

Jennifer Brout: I am very excited to speak to you about your findings! To me, the finding that misophonia has a very specific neural signature adds important evidence to the idea that it is a standalone disorder. Am I understanding that correctly?

Heather Hansen: Yes, this neural signature is different than what we see in anxiety and other disorders. Our main finding is that the anterior insula, part of the salience network, is highly involved in misophonia.

JB: Then, point one gives us more evidence that misophonia involves the anterior insula?

HH: Yes, but in addition, we found that the anterior insula gets more connected the more severe your misophonia is. So that connectivity changes or increases as a function of misophonia level.

JB: Are you saying that if you have more severe misophonia, the connectivity of the insula will appear greater?

HH: Yes. Correct. Plus, the idea that more connectivity is associated with more severe misophonia may lead us to characterize the disorder as being on a spectrum rather than a binary diagnosis of ‘you have it’ or ‘you don’t.’

JB: Are these connections a result of having misophonia, or does the greater connectivity cause more severe misophonia?

HH: We don't know yet. FMRI does not show directionality. I can just say that those things are associated in some way. Keep in mind, however, that measuring the insula and its connectivity is not a perfect science. Researchers use different equipment and define brain areas in different ways.

JB: Thank you for pointing that out. That is something we don't think about very much!

HH: So that's an important nuance—in a lot of the neuroimaging papers we have currently out, we all locate brain regions slightly differently. In addition, because the anterior insula is involved in so many different things, different sections of it belong to many different brain networks. It's part of a salience network that helps us attend to the things that are important. But it also has sections that are part of networks linked to motor processing and sensations, and the default mode (which is what your brain is doing when you don't have a specific task).

article continues after advertisement

JB: I see.

HH: All of this is to say, I wanted to investigate the specificity of the anterior insula a little bit more to figure out what part of it is the crucial part in misophonia. Therefore, I divided the insula in a couple of different ways so that I could test the parts out – the part of the insula involved in the salience network, the part involved in the default mode network, etc. Turns out there is only increased connectivity from the part of the insula that belongs to the salience network in misophonia.

JB: How does this compare to previous studies?

HH: One of the things that I learned, which adds evidence to some of the earlier neuroimaging work (like Schroeder et al. and Kumar et al.’s work), is that the salience network definitely seems to be involved. This paper basically adds some specific data to their earlier hypotheses and says, yes. It seems to be that it's the salience part of the anterior insula that's important in misophonia.

JB: Would you sum this up a little?

HH: The anterior insula is a part of the brain that communicates with other brain regions more in misophonia. It communicates with higher-level auditory regions to understand what a complex sound is. It communicates with attention regions to determine if one should pay attention to a particular sound. It communicates with an integration region that helps compare sounds to prior experiences. It's a higher-level region that communicates with a lot of other regions in the brain, regions that seem particularly relevant for misophonia. And this communication happens more in folks with more severe misophonia.

JB: Misophonia, then, has to do with various brain areas, and the anterior insula (part of the salience network) is highly important. The more this anterior insula connects to other areas may determine the severity of the disorder.

HH: Yes.

JB: Thank you very much for taking the time to do this interview and for all of your great work on misophonia! I am looking forward to your next study!

item.title: Benzodiazepines, Kratom, and the Search for Relief in Midlife
item.description:
Midlife

Benzodiazepines, Kratom, and the Search for Relief in Midlife

Why midlife anxiety calls for a closer look at the reasons women seek relief.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Midlife anxiety may have hormonal, psychological, medical, or situational causes.
  • Benzodiazepines can provide relief but carry risks including dependence and withdrawal.
  • Women seeking relief may turn to kratom, which varies in potency and carries health risks.
  • Understanding the source of distress can lead to more comprehensive treatment.

By Jana Wu, LCSW, LADC, ICAADC, CASAC

I have worked in mental health and substance use treatment for more than 15 years. As I approach 50, I keep returning to a question that feels both personal and professional: Why are we so quick to relieve women’s distress before we fully understand it?

Kratom is part of what brought this question into sharper focus for me.

I have met and worked with many women from their late 30s into their 60s who stumbled onto kratom while searching for relief from anxiety or pain. Many describe another benefit as well: energy. They often describe it not simply as a way to feel better, but as a way to keep functioning in lives that already feel stretched to their limits.

They tell me kratom helped them work, exercise, keep up with their children, care for aging parents, and continue meeting the demands of daily life.

Listening to these women has made me think about the much longer history of women, anxiety, and substances that promise relief.

A Long History of Treating Women’s Distress

The medical response to women’s anxiety did not begin with benzodiazepines. In the 19th century, diagnoses such as hysteria and neurasthenia were used to explain symptoms including anxiety, fatigue, insomnia, irritability, and pain. By the mid-20th century, sedatives were followed by tranquilizers, such as Miltown, and eventually benzodiazepines.

Valium, introduced in 1963, became the top-selling prescription medication in the United States for years. Its association with women’s distress became prominent enough to enter popular culture. In 1966, the Rolling Stones released “Mother’s Little Helper,” a song about a woman relying on prescribed tranquilizers to cope with the pressures of family life, domestic responsibilities, and aging.

Nearly 60 years later, the reference is striking. The medications have changed, but the question remains: What happens when the distress does not?

When Relief Is Not Enough

Benzodiazepines can provide essential relief and have a legitimate place in medicine. But relief is not the same as a long-term treatment plan. Benzodiazepines carry risks including physical dependence and potentially dangerous withdrawal.

For women in midlife, this becomes particularly important. Perimenopause can bring or intensify anxiety, sleep disruption, and changes in mood while many women are simultaneously managing careers, children, aging parents, relationships, and enormous expectations of themselves.

Yet, our health care system is often better equipped to quiet a symptom than to understand the life surrounding it.

Understanding why a woman suddenly cannot sleep, why panic has appeared for the first time, or why she no longer feels at home in her own body requires curiosity and patience. It means considering what may be hormonal, psychological, medical, or situational before simply trying to make the symptom disappear.

Why Kratom Deserves Our Attention

I am not suggesting that benzodiazepines cause women to use kratom. These pathways are far more complicated than that.

But I hear enough stories of women searching for relief from anxiety, pain, insomnia, fatigue, and other symptoms to believe we should pay much closer attention to how they arrived there.

For some, kratom may represent another chapter in a long history of medicating women’s distress. For others, it may feel like an attempt to reclaim control by choosing something perceived as natural, traditional, and outside the pharmaceutical system.

But “natural” should not be confused with predictable or risk-free. Kratom products in the United States are not regulated like FDA-approved medications and can vary substantially in potency.

From a substance use treatment perspective, another concern is what people may be using alongside kratom. I see individuals who use kratom while also drinking alcohol, taking prescribed benzodiazepines, or using opioids. Combining substances with sedating or opioid effects can increase the risk of dangerous interactions, including excessive sedation and respiratory depression. This is a risk I do not think we talk about enough.

The point is not that benzodiazepines lead women to kratom, nor that kratom is the answer. It is that women continue searching for relief.

Whose Discomfort Are We Treating?

We need to offer women more than a choice between enduring severe anxiety and relying indefinitely on a substance to make it disappear.

Providers should also ask themselves a difficult question: Whose discomfort are we treating?

Women’s anxiety should not be minimized. But neither should every manifestation of it be treated as something that must disappear immediately.

As clinicians and researchers learn more about kratom and kratom use disorder, we should listen carefully to how women arrived there. Sometimes that story began years earlier, with a woman who was anxious, a provider who wanted to help, and a prescription that offered relief.

The harder question is what happens when relief becomes the treatment plan.

Contributor Bio

Jana Wu, LCSW, LADC, ICAADC, CASAC, is a clinician at Mountainside Treatment Center specializing in PTSD, anxiety, depression, and co-occurring disorders. A nationally recognized expert on kratom, she founded the country’s first clinician-led kratom support group and has presented on kratom and emerging substances to professional audiences nationwide. Her expertise has been featured in The Wall Street Journal, Rolling Stone, and on NBC News and iHeartRadio. She was a founder of the Addictions Committee of the Connecticut chapter of the National Association of Social Workers.

item.title: Why Everything Feels Like Too Much
item.description:
Stress

Why Everything Feels Like Too Much

Modern life asks us to carry too much. Here’s how to make the load smaller.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Overwhelm may come from the scale of what we are trying to carry.
  • Modern life expands what we can see, monitor, compare, and worry about.
  • Shortening the time horizon can make daily demands feel more manageable.
  • Making life smaller can help us engage more fully with what is in front of us.

There is something about this time of year that seems to accelerate life.

As routines resume and schedules fill, overwhelm can seem almost built into the season. The feeling is especially visible on campuses and in families preparing for a new school year, but it is hardly confined to them. Across work, home, and daily life, many of us are moving from the relative looseness of summer into a period of greater structure, expectation, and demand.

We often assume that overwhelm simply means we have too much to do. Yet there may be another dimension to it. Modern life has dramatically expanded what we are able to see, know, monitor, anticipate, compare, and worry about.

The question may be less about how many tasks are on our lists and more about how much of the world we are trying to carry at once — and how we can bring that load back to a more manageable size.

When the World Seems Bigger

A recent review in Behavioral Sciences by Jose Yong and colleagues offers an intriguing way to think about this experience. The researchers examine contemporary psychological stress through the lens of evolutionary mismatch, the idea that characteristics that developed under one set of environmental conditions may function differently when those conditions change dramatically (Yong et al., 2026).

Human beings have always faced stress, uncertainty, competition, and social comparison. What is unusual today is the scale and reach of those experiences. Our social worlds can include thousands of people. We can learn about disasters or conflicts anywhere on Earth within minutes, remain connected to work nearly continuously, and compare our accomplishments, appearance, parenting, homes, vacations, and happiness with people we have never met.

The Yong paper raises an important possibility: Some of what we experience as overwhelming may be a reasonable response to an environment whose scale has expanded extraordinarily quickly.

As an epidemiologist, I find this perspective compelling because epidemiology encourages us to look beyond the person experiencing an outcome and examine the surrounding conditions and exposures. When we feel overwhelmed, then, it may be useful to ask: Has the scale of what I am trying to hold become larger than what actually requires my attention?

There are several ways to bring that scale back to a more manageable size.

1. Shorten the Time Horizon

One reason this time of year can feel overwhelming is that we begin mentally experiencing the entire fall before it has happened. We think simultaneously about the semester, the school year, deadlines, the family calendar, upcoming travel, unfinished projects, and problems that may arise weeks or months from now.

A useful question is: What actually needs something from me today?

Many things deserve planning, but planning for October does not require psychologically living in October. Narrowing attention to the next appropriate step can make a large mental landscape considerably more manageable.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes that prolonged stress can affect concentration, sleep, decision-making, and health. Adequate rest, movement, recovery, and manageable priorities all support our ability to respond to demanding circumstances (CDC, 2026).

2. Narrow the Field of Responsibility

Modern communication makes us aware of far more than we can personally influence. We encounter problems in our families, workplaces, communities, country, and world, often in the same stream of information.

It can help to distinguish among what requires action from us, what we may be able to influence, and what we are simply aware of. Caring deeply about something does not require giving it continuous attention, and recognizing a problem does not automatically make us responsible for resolving it.

We can remain informed and engaged while becoming more deliberate about where our limited attention and energy can actually make a difference.

3. Shrink the Comparison Group

One of the most interesting ideas in the Yong paper concerns competition and social comparison.

Human beings have always paid attention to status, accomplishment, belonging, and how we are doing relative to others. What has changed is the size of the population available for comparison. Digital life allows us to measure our careers, parenting, bodies, homes, productivity, or happiness against an almost limitless collection of highly visible examples.

Comparison can motivate us and expand our sense of possibility, but an enormous reference group can also quietly raise our standards until ordinary accomplishment or contentment begins to feel inadequate.

A useful question is: Is comparison changing my definition of enough?

Becoming more conscious of whose standards shape our own can restore a sense of proportion.

4. Create Limits Where There Are None

Many features of contemporary life provide few natural stopping points. There is always another email, headline, notification, activity, meeting, or task. Work can follow us home, family schedules can absorb every open evening, and our phones can make events occurring anywhere in the world feel immediately present.

When the environment provides few boundaries, we may need to establish some ourselves. This can mean choosing when to read the news, leaving some evenings unscheduled, turning off unnecessary notifications, protecting time away from work, or allowing a message that does not require an immediate answer to wait until tomorrow.

The U.S. Surgeon General's workplace well-being framework similarly emphasizes work-life boundaries, rest, autonomy, social connection, and organizational conditions that support well-being (Office of the Surgeon General, 2022). These principles remind us that overwhelm is shaped by more than individual behavior. Families, workplaces, schools, and institutions can also examine whether the environments they create are asking people to carry more than is necessary.

Make Life Smaller When It Feels Too Big

Modern life gives us extraordinary access to information, people, opportunities, and events throughout the world. That access enriches our lives, but it also requires us to be more deliberate about what deserves our attention.

As the new academic and school year begins, we do not need to mentally live the entire fall in September. We can focus on what genuinely needs our attention now, be more selective about what we carry, and notice when comparison or constant input begins to distort our sense of what is enough.

Making life smaller does not mean withdrawing from the world. It means engaging with it at a scale that leaves room for the people, responsibilities, and experiences directly in front of us.

The larger world will still be there tomorrow, and we may be better able to meet it when it arrives.

item.title: Tuning In to Joy and Finding the Spark
item.description:
Education

Tuning In to Joy and Finding the Spark

Joy can be the catalyst for growth, persistence, and learning.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Joy isn't just a result of achievement—it can be the catalyst that sparks growth.
  • Engaging with the arts provides a creative sandbox that turns learning friction into deep fulfillment.
  • We can recognize unexpected moments of joy or intentionally cultivate conditions for joy to appear.
Source: kmcfadzen/Childsplayeducation/Used with permission

This is Part 1 of a series.

Every attempt at the same note ended in frustration. Lauren van Huisstede, an Arizona State University researcher and co-author of this series, loved the rich, resonant sound of the cello. As an adult, she decided to learn the instrument for herself. For months, practice became a lesson in persistence, but one note on the D string—a stubborn F sharp—seemed impossible to produce cleanly.

One day, something changed.

"I realized I just needed to shift my fingers slightly forward,” she shares, “changing the angle that the pads of my fingers press into the string ever so slightly. I took up my bow, drew it across the string, and lo and behold… a clear, ringing F sharp. I felt joy, peace, and pride."

A clear note, vibrating through the fingers, ringing true. A moment of joy.

Her moment of joy didn’t lead to mastering the cello. She was (and still very much is) a beginner. The joy came from discovery, from finally hearing what was possible, and it made her want to keep going.

We often think of joy as the destination, something that comes after we achieve our goals. Maybe we have it backwards? What if joy isn't the destination at all? Maybe joy is the catalyst to help us get there?

Defining Joy

Joy is surprisingly difficult to define. We often use it interchangeably with happiness, although the experiences aren't quite the same. Happiness can describe a broader sense that life is going well. Joy is often more immediate: I am fully alive in this moment. It pulls us into the present, inviting discovery, connection, and engagement.

Joy is deeply experiential, pulling us completely into the present moment. Active rather than passive, joy invites discovery, connection, and continued engagement.

There are at least two complementary ways to think about joy.

Joy doesn’t always announce itself. Sometimes it simply appears: a child's uncontrollable laughter, a breathtaking harmony during a concert, a shared smile with a stranger, a single cello note finally ringing true after months of practice. These moments cannot be planned or manufactured; they simply appear, asking us to notice them.

This is when joy can be recognized. Some of life's most memorable moments arrive unexpectedly. Moments of joy invite us to revel in them. All we have to do is accept the invitation.

We don’t have to wait for these moments to appear, either; we can create them. Joy can be cultivated. We cannot force ourselves to feel joyful on command, but we can intentionally create conditions to inspire joy. We can choose the music that accompanies our mornings and fill our living spaces with art that inspires us. Sing in the car, dance in the kitchen, try something new just for fun. These small, intentional acts don't guarantee joy. That's not really how joy works. They create the conditions for discovery, connection, and surprise.

Source: Juan Patino Photography/Mozart for Munchkins/Used with permission
Source: Sara Sherman/Mozart for Munchkins/Used with permission

Why Does Joy Matter?

Joy does far more than make us feel good.

By making the intentional choice to experience joy today, we build the psychological, social, and physical resources that help us adapt to future challenges.

We can be the conductors of our lives. Beyond just experiencing the passive, transactional joy that is essential in life, we might benefit more by deliberately taking action to build moments of joy.

Joy acts as a shock absorber for the rough patches of life, breaking the monotony and actively recharging our resilience batteries. When we experience joy, we become more motivated to persist through difficulty, more open to new ideas, and more connected to the people around us. It reminds us that when it feels like we are surviving day to day, we are fully alive.

Lauren's cello story illustrates this beautifully. Mastering F sharp sparked further learning; it transformed the learning process itself. That single moment of joy fueled countless hours of future practice.

The arts provide some of our most powerful pathways into these experiences.

Music, for example, is far more than background entertainment. It is an intentional tool that shapes our minds and bodies. Listening to music can reduce stress hormones such as cortisol, synchronize physiological rhythms, and influence emotion before we consciously recognize the change. A familiar melody can transport us back decades, while a new composition can awaken curiosity and wonder. Music is continually transforming us.

Drama offers another pathway into joy. We are moved by watching performances and by participating in them. Stepping into another character's perspective, collaborating with other performers, or witnessing life as a story unfolds invites deep emotional engagement. These shared artistic experiences create opportunities for connection, empathy, and discovery in ways few other activities can.

Source: Sara Sherman/Mozart for Munchkins/Used with permission

Oh, to Joy!

Consider one thing in your life that feels especially difficult right now. Rather than asking how you'll feel once you've overcome it, ask yourself a different question: Where might a small moment of joy already exist?

Try putting on a favorite song before a difficult task. Take just five minutes to draw, sing, dance, get silly with a child or friend. Notice the conversation that makes you smile or the satisfaction of getting something right. When those moments happen, stay and notice for a moment what happens next.

Do you want to keep going? Does the difficult thing feel slightly different? Are you more curious or willing to try again? Joy has no finish line.

It can even spring from a small, intentional adjustment—a finger moved slightly forward on a cello string—before the note rings clear.

These tiny adjustments are often what make our goals possible. Those joyful moments may be a part of what makes reaching them possible.

In this series, we’re collaborating with Jenny Millinger, Associate Artistic Director at Childsplay Theatre Company in Tempe, Arizona, and Lauren van Huisstede and Katie Bernstein, researchers from Arizona State University (ASU), to explore the role of the arts and joy in learning and well-being. This intersection of joy, learning, and the arts is at the heart of their work at Literacy@Play, a research-practice partnership between ASU and Childsplay. Together, we will explore what science tells us about joy, why the arts are uniquely positioned to spark it, and how intentionally cultivating joyful experiences can transform the way we learn, work, and live.

item.title: "Black People Don't Hang Themselves" Is Both Right and Wrong
item.description:
Suicide

"Black People Don't Hang Themselves" Is Both Right and Wrong

Why the response to Black suicides is historically accurate, and what we're missing.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • At least seven Black people have been found hanging under disputed circumstances in the U.S. in 2026 alone.
  • Suicide deaths among Black Americans rose 53% from 2014 to 2024, far outpacing every other group.
  • Racism operates as chronic stress, driving suicide risk along with hypertension, stroke, and early death.

I was mid-lecture in my undergraduate community psychology class the week the Raleigh case broke. I was standing at the front of the room talking about ambiguous loss and retaliation killings, of all things, when a student's phone lit up with a headline about a young Black man found hanging near a downtown parking lot, just blocks from a Caribbean festival. By the time class ended, three more students had pulled it up and we were in a full-on discussion. Within the hour, my own timeline was full of stories about and responses to the discovery of the Charlotte teenager with a ratchet strap around her neck, 10 days after she went missing. Then, the familiar sting when we realized that no autopsy was ordered. We talked about the Delta State student whose family fought for a second look. We talked about the six, maybe seven, more that we had seen either on the news or on social media in 2026.

And right alongside the grief, the same response started appearing everywhere: "Black people don't hang themselves." Ms. Rachel said it out loud on video. I heard it on one of my favorite podcasts, and it was even said in a group chat that is typically reserved for humor but was not exempt from this tough conversation.

Source: Isha Metzger

I get why we say it. "Black people don't hang themselves” is said not out of paranoia, but due to a harsh reality of racism in our distant and recent history. Lynching is inside the bodies of our country, and it’s alive in people who are still here, passed down through generations of stories and repeated experiences. When Black bodies show up hanging in public spaces and cases are closed in 72 hours with no autopsy, no phone recovered, no interview with the person who found the body, and seemingly no questions asked (as some reporters suggest happened in the Charlotte case), communities are not being paranoid, suspicious, or irrational when they ask questions.

Families like Nolan Wells’s and Trey Reed's pursuing independent autopsies, and organizations like the NAACP Legal Defense Fund calling for transparency, represent us doing the due diligence the justice system has failed to do, not us participating in or fueling some unwarranted conspiracy. Most of these cases genuinely deserve more scrutiny than they receive.

As a clinician who has spent two decades in this work, here's where the nuance comes in for me: While we've been organizing around the deaths we suspect are homicides, I don’t want us to stop talking about how suicide is actually a real threat to the Black community as well.

Because the numbers are not small, and they are not stable. They are rising at alarming rates.

Between 2014 and 2024, the suicide death rate among Black Americans climbed 53%, which is more than 10 times faster than the rate for white Americans over the same decade. Black boys and young men are now dying by suicide at a rate that outpaces white boys and young men in the same age range, something that would have been almost unthinkable a generation ago. The crisis peaks between ages 20 and 24. Earlier CDC data showed that suicide among Black youth ages 10 to 24 jumped by more than a third in just three years.

I train clinicians for a living. I've sat across from more than one brilliant, high-functioning Black graduate student who showed up early, over-prepared, and never asked for a deadline extension; and I watched them minimize their own suicidal thoughts because some part of them had absorbed the same myth we're now shouting online: "I'm not the type" or "We don't do that." I've had to gently and directly ask the question anyway, every time, because the data and my own clinical experience tells me the myth is now more dangerous than the stigma it was supposed to protect us from.

So, I want us to hold space for knowing that both things can be true at once. Yes, some of these public hanging deaths deserve more independent investigation and attention, and families are right to demand it. And also: Racism is killing us through channels we're far more comfortable naming as murder than as slow violence. The chronic stress of discrimination is linked to hypertension, stroke, and accelerated biological aging. Black maternal mortality remains a national emergency. Police violence shortens life expectancy for entire communities, not just the people directly harmed. Suicide is one more branch on that same tree: racial trauma, untreated depression, and a mental health system that still doesn't reach us the way it should, all converging.

Denying that suicide happens to us doesn't protect us. It just means fewer of us get help before it's too late.

So this Suicide Prevention Month, I'm asking you to hold both truths in the same hand. Keep asking hard questions about the cases that don't add up. And also check on your strong friend, your high-achieving cousin, or the deacon who never misses a Sunday. Ask directly, "Are you OK? Are you thinking about hurting yourself?" As a clinician, mother, aunt, and friend, I promise you, directness saves lives, it doesn't plant ideas. Save 988 in your phone right now, not when you think you or a friend will need it.

We don't have to choose between grieving what might be lynching and grieving what is suicide. Both are killing us. Both deserve our full attention.

Source: Isha Metzger

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
